stem: A 62 year old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is started on a medication that blocks the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Three weeks later he develops a persistent dry cough. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

options.D: Increased histamine release from mast cells

why.A: ACE is also kininase II, the enzyme that breaks down bradykinin. Blocking it lets bradykinin and substance P build up in the airway, causing dry cough and angioedema. An ARB avoids this because it does not affect bradykinin.
why.B: ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II. High angiotensin II would raise blood pressure and would not cause a cough.
why.C: Low aldosterone does cause hyperkalemia, a real ACE inhibitor effect, but it does not cause cough.
why.D: Histamine drives allergic reactions. ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema are bradykinin mediated, not mast cell mediated.
why.E: Renin rises reflexively when angiotensin II falls, but this is not the cause of the cough.

takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema come from bradykinin. Switch to an ARB.

stem: A 24 year old woman presents with 3 days of persistent vomiting. She is lightheaded and has dry mucous membranes. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.52, PaCO2 48 mm Hg, and HCO3 38 mEq/L. Urine chloride is low. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

why.C: This is chloride responsive metabolic alkalosis. Vomiting loses gastric HCl and causes volume contraction, and a low urine chloride confirms it. Saline restores volume and chloride so the kidney can excrete bicarbonate. Replace potassium too, since it is usually low.
why.A: Acetazolamide promotes bicarbonate excretion and is used for alkalosis with volume overload. This patient is volume depleted.
why.B: Loop diuretics worsen volume contraction and make the alkalosis worse.
why.D: Blocking aldosterone does not restore volume or chloride and would add to the volume loss.
why.E: Thiazides cause volume loss and hypochloremic alkalosis, so they worsen this picture.

takeaway: Low urine chloride means chloride responsive alkalosis. Fix it with saline and potassium.

stem: A 55 year old man presents with 40 minutes of crushing chest pain. Blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg and heart rate is 62/min. He has jugular venous distension and clear lungs. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following should be avoided in this patient?

why.B: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, JVD, and clear lungs suggests right ventricular infarction. The RV is preload dependent, so nitrates can cause profound hypotension. Avoid nitrates and diuretics, and confirm with right sided leads (V4R).
why.A: Aspirin is indicated in STEMI unless the patient is allergic.
why.C: Fluids are appropriate in RV infarction to maintain preload.
why.D: Anticoagulation is part of standard STEMI care.
why.E: Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy.

takeaway: Inferior STEMI plus hypotension and clear lungs: check V4R and avoid nitrates.

stem: A 3 year old unvaccinated boy is brought in with 6 hours of high fever, drooling, and a muffled voice. He sits leaning forward with his chin out and has inspiratory stridor. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Examine the oropharynx with a tongue depressor
options.C: Secure the airway in a controlled setting with anesthesia and ENT
options.D: Start IV antibiotics and observe on the ward

why.C: This is epiglottitis, classically from Haemophilus influenzae type b in an unvaccinated child. The priority is a secure airway in a controlled setting, such as the operating room with anesthesia and ENT ready. Give antibiotics like ceftriaxone after the airway is secured.
why.A: A neck film can show the thumb sign, but sending an unstable child to radiology risks sudden obstruction.
why.B: Agitating the child or examining the throat can trigger laryngospasm and complete obstruction.
why.D: Antibiotics are needed, but they do not come before airway control.
why.E: Racemic epinephrine treats croup. It does not reliably fix fixed supraglottic swelling.

takeaway: Suspected epiglottitis: keep the child calm and secure the airway first.
kind: emergency medicine in service exam style, pediatrics

stem: A 28 year old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision. Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg, heart rate is 132/min, and oxygen saturation is 86%. He has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the right, and tracheal deviation to the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Immediate needle or finger decompression of the right chest

why.B: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Hypotension, hypoxia, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds mean air is trapped under pressure and blocking venous return. Decompress immediately with a needle or finger thoracostomy, then place a chest tube.
why.C: CT is unsafe and unnecessary in an unstable patient with a clear diagnosis.
why.D: Positive pressure ventilation can worsen a tension pneumothorax.
why.E: Tamponade also causes distended neck veins and hypotension, but breath sounds are normal and the trachea is midline.

takeaway: Hypotension plus absent breath sounds plus JVD: decompress first, image never.

stem: A 19 year old college student presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash on the trunk. Lumbar puncture shows gram negative diplococci. His roommate asks about preventive treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis for close contacts?

why.A: This is Neisseria meningitidis. Close contacts such as household members, roommates, and people exposed to oral secretions need prophylaxis. Rifampin for 2 days, or a single dose of ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone, eliminates nasopharyngeal carriage.
why.B: Vancomycin is an IV drug for resistant gram positive infections and is not used for prophylaxis.
why.C: Amoxicillin does not reliably clear meningococcal carriage.
why.E: Doxycycline is not a recommended regimen for meningococcal prophylaxis.

takeaway: Meningococcal contacts get rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone. The patient gets ceftriaxone.

stem: A 71 year old man with atrial fibrillation takes warfarin. On a routine lab check his INR is 12.4. He has no bleeding and no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
options.D: Continue warfarin and repeat INR in 1 week

why.A: With an INR above 10 and no bleeding, hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K, then recheck the INR. Oral vitamin K works well and avoids the anaphylaxis risk of IV dosing.
why.B: FFP is not first line, takes large volumes, and is only used for bleeding when PCC is not available.
why.C: PCC is for major or life threatening bleeding that needs immediate reversal.
why.D: Continuing warfarin with an INR this high risks serious bleeding.
why.E: Warfarin does not affect platelets, so transfusing them does not help.

takeaway: High INR without bleeding: hold warfarin and give vitamin K. With major bleeding: PCC plus IV vitamin K.
kind: internal medicine in service exam style, hematology

stem: A 26 year old woman presents with 6 hours of severe lower abdominal pain and light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. Blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg and heart rate is 128/min. The abdomen is tender and urine hCG is positive. Bedside ultrasound shows free fluid in the hepatorenal space. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

why.D: Hypotension with a positive pregnancy test and free fluid in Morison pouch means ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. She needs resuscitation, blood products as needed, and emergent surgery.
why.A: Methotrexate is for stable, unruptured ectopic pregnancy that meets criteria.
why.B: Serial hCG is for stable patients.
why.C: An unstable patient should not wait for further imaging.
why.E: Expectant management is only for stable patients with a low and falling hCG.

takeaway: Unstable with a positive hCG and free fluid: ruptured ectopic, go to the OR.

stem: A 52 year old woman with chronic alcohol use is admitted with confusion and a serum sodium of 108 mEq/L. Treatment raises her sodium to 128 mEq/L over 12 hours. Four days later she develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and flaccid quadriparesis, with preserved vertical eye movements and blinking. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

why.B: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too fast (more than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours) shrinks brain cells and demyelinates the pons. Delayed onset after correction, with dysarthria, dysphagia, and quadriparesis (locked in), is classic. Alcohol use, malnutrition, and liver disease raise the risk.
why.A: Wernicke causes confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency. It does not follow sodium correction.
why.C: This can also cause locked in syndrome, but the timing after rapid sodium correction points to osmotic demyelination.
why.D: Guillain Barre causes ascending weakness with areflexia after an infection. It would not follow sodium correction.
why.E: Cerebral edema is the risk of hyponatremia itself, not of rapid correction.

takeaway: Correct chronic hyponatremia slowly, no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours in high risk patients.

stem: A 41 year old farmworker is brought in after spraying pesticides without protective equipment. He has diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation, diarrhea, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, and muscle fasciculations. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment?

why.A: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing excess acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects and is titrated to dry bronchial secretions. Pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme and works best early. Remove clothing and decontaminate.
why.B: Physostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen the toxicity.
why.C: Naloxone reverses opioids, which cause miosis and respiratory depression but not bronchorrhea and fasciculations.
why.E: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning.

takeaway: Cholinergic toxidrome: atropine until the lungs are dry, plus pralidoxime.
kind: emergency medicine in service exam style, toxicology
